headline: Rattlesnake Grounds Still Paying, Bunker Schools Set the Table at the Hook
subhead: Warm water is stretching the fluke bite deep into fall while Harvest Moon tides push bait — and bigger bass — toward Sandy Hook.
body_markdown:
The call this week is a split day, and it's an easy one to make. Start on the Rattlesnake Grounds or the drift lanes off the Highlands on the first half of the tide, then run up toward Flynn's Knoll and the Hook as the bunker schools push through on the back half. That's where the bay's putting its money right now, and the reasoning is simple: the water's still holding onto summer longer than it should, and the Harvest Moon's bigger swings are moving bait around fast enough to concentrate fish where the structure lines up.

Raritan Bay hasn't cooled off the way late September usually demands. That warmer-than-normal water is keeping fluke shallower and more aggressive than they have any business being this deep into the season, and it's why keeper counts around the Highlands and the Rattlesnake Grounds have actually gotten better over the last few weeks instead of falling off like they typically do once the nights turn. Sea bass are mixing in on the same structure, which tells you the whole zone is running about two to three weeks behind its usual fall clock. Enjoy it while it lasts — the first real cold front that gets through will tighten this up fast.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the keeper-class stripers would start showing up behind the first wave of smaller migrant fish as more bait got pushed out of the back bays, and that's exactly what the dock talk out of Atlantic Highlands and the Keyport ramps is confirming now. The schoolie run that's been working the Highlands and the mouth of the Navesink for two weeks is starting to show heavier fish mixed in, and bunker are staging thick enough in the bay that the next wave setting up around Sandy Hook should be more than just blitzing snapper blues and short bass.

On the fluke side, the program hasn't changed, just tightened up. Drift the Rattlesnake Grounds and the deeper edges off the Highlands in 25 to 40 feet, working the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. White and chartreuse 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails are getting it done on the drift, but the guys putting bigger fish in the box are switching over to live bait once they find a patch of fish — snapper bunker, spot, and killies on a simple fluke rig with just enough weight to stay on bottom through the sweep. Sea bass are coming up on the same drifts around any hard bottom or rockpile, so it's worth dropping a bucktail tipped with squid if the fluke bite goes quiet for a stretch.

The bass and blue pattern is building around bait, not structure, right now, which means location changes day to day. Bunker pods have been holding in the middle of the bay and along the edges of the Flats off Keyport, and when the tide starts pulling them toward the mouth of the bay, that's when things get active around Flynn's Knoll, Romer Shoal, and the deeper edge of the Rip at the Hook. Chunk bunker on a fish-finder rig fished tight to bottom on the last two hours of the ebb has been the most consistent producer for stripers in that 24 to 32-inch range, with the occasional bigger fish mixed in. Topwater walk-the-dog plugs and 2-ounce metal are worth keeping rigged for the moments bait gets pushed to the surface — it's not an all-day blitz situation yet, but the schools are dense enough that it can turn on fast for twenty or thirty minutes at a time.

Bluefish are riding along with every one of those bunker pods, and the size has been ticking up as bigger fish move in behind the snappers that have been thick in the Navesink and Shrewsbury all month. Anything from 3 to 6 pounds is showing on bunker chunks and diamond jigs worked through the deeper holes off the Highlands, and that should only get more aggressive as the bigger tides this week keep flushing bait out of the rivers and into open water.

Keyport Flats is still worth a stop for stripers working the channel edges on bunker chunks or fresh clam, especially on the top of the incoming when bait gets pushed up onto the shallower sand. It's not a numbers game out there right now — more a patient, well-placed bait kind of bite — but the fish that are coming through have some size to them.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern holds as long as the warm water does. If a real cold front pushes through late this week like the long-range signs suggest, expect the fluke bite to tighten up fast and the striper migration to accelerate — more fish moving through quicker rather than holding and feeding. Until that happens, the smart play is fluke early on the Rattlesnake and Highlands drifts, then position for bunker-driven bass and blues at the Hook as the tide pushes bait through Flynn's Knoll and Romer Shoal on the second half of the day. Keep an eye on the moon-driven tides — the bigger swings this week are doing a lot of the work moving bait, and that's the whole engine behind everything biting right now.
